ratings.plot: A guide leads two men through an area known as the Zone to find a room that grants wishes.

verdict.reason: See it theatrically while you can—this is Tarkovsky's most immersive film. The sound design and long takes demand the focus that only a darkened theater provides.

ratings.plot: Filmed at night from Tel Aviv rooftops, this investigative documentary examines the civilian casualties of Israel's military operations in Gaza and the systems behind targeted killings of Palestinians.

verdict.reason: Essential testimony from the people who built Israel's targeting systems, shot in the dark on Tel Aviv rooftops. The 80-minute runtime keeps the weight intact without padding.

movies.title: ONCE UPON A TIME IN HARLEM

ratings.plot: A decade post-death, filmmaker William Greaves reveals his final work: footage of a 1972 gathering he arranged with Harlem Renaissance legends, which he deemed his most significant capture.

verdict.reason: A lost Greaves documentary surfaces with pristine restoration at Lincoln Center. Rare archival footage of Harlem Renaissance figures in 1972 makes this essential cinema history.

ratings.plot: Paul Thomas Anderson captures Brooklyn musician Cameron Winter's minimalist performance in this striking concert film, blending intimate close-ups with sweeping shots of the vast venue, all shot on 16mm and 35mm film.

verdict.reason: Paul Thomas Anderson shot a 72-minute concert film on 35mm and 16mm for a performer whose album dominated year-end lists. See it theatrical before it vanishes.

ratings.plot: Four strangers' paths cross by chance, leading to complex emotional entanglements that challenge their existing relationships and force them to confront uncomfortable truths about love and commitment.

verdict.reason: Lee Chang-dong's first film in a decade demands the big screen and your full attention. Nearly three hours of moral complexity and emotional precision—see it before word spreads.

ratings.plot: A hard-partying New York City club promoter sees his whirlwind lifestyle upended by the arrival of the 10-year-old son he never knew he had.

verdict.reason: Firstman's debut balances comedy and genuine heart around an unexpected father-son story. A rare new film playing Lincoln Center that earns its two-hour runtime.

ratings.plot: Thirty-four days before she's sent to prison, notorious Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move. What begins as an intimate portrait becomes a mind-bending three-year journey.

verdict.reason: Watch it. Fielding and Oppenheim pull off a three-year documentary experiment that turns a famous fraud case into something genuinely unpredictable.

ratings.plot: A filmmaker applies lessons from a Hallmark movie writing workshop to pitch a documentary about concrete.

verdict.reason: John Wilson's deadpan conceptual comedy deserves the big screen. A Hallmark workshop applied to concrete is the kind of absurdist premise only he executes this well.

ratings.plot: Follows a mother, her daughter, and a teenage boy blamed for a tragic death as they travel to Tenerife together, confronting grief, blame, and forgiveness on a family holiday that never happened.

verdict.reason: Sandra Wollner's chamber drama about grief and blame deserves the theater. The 121-minute runtime and intimate character work demand full attention on a big screen.

ratings.plot: Odysseus, king of Ithaca, embarks on a perilous journey to return home after the Trojan War.

verdict.reason: Nolan's 172-minute epic demands a theater, and 70mm or IMAX is the only way to see it. The scale and ambition justify the subway trip and the runtime.

ratings.plot: In an increasingly Westernized postwar Tokyo, an aging widower arranges a marriage for his only daughter.

verdict.reason: Ozu's final film is essential—a masterwork of stillness and domestic grace at a major venue. Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see the precise geometry of every frame.

ratings.plot: A young woman is followed by an unknown supernatural force after a sexual encounter.

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical screening of one of the great horror films of the 2010s. Mitchell's precise direction and unsettling sound design demand the big screen and dark room.

ratings.plot: In 19th century Massachusetts, the March sisters--Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy--on the threshold of womanhood, go through many ups and downs in life and endeavor to make important decisions about their futures.

verdict.reason: Gerwig's take on this story justifies the trip, especially on Metrograph's screen. The 135-minute runtime and formal precision reward theatrical attention.

movies.title: The Flavor of Green Tea Over Rice

ratings.plot: A childless middle-aged couple faces a marital crisis.

verdict.reason: Essential Ozu on 35mm at Metrograph. A masterwork about marriage and compromise that demands the big screen.

ratings.plot: A group of high school students sets off on a school trip to discover the ruins of Pompeii. They are seized by a sense of vertigo. They allow themselves to be overwhelmed by desire and anger, until they surrender completely.

verdict.reason: A rare debut that justifies the hype—Pompeii's ruins become a stage for teenage vertigo and desire. Atlan's control of mood and image demands the big screen at Lincoln Center.

ratings.plot: CIA agents Chris and Lee face a trust-testing mission from Santiago to Easter Island during 1973 in Chile.

verdict.reason: Martin McDonagh's latest is a sharp spy comedy that earns its runtime. The 1973 Chile setting and fractious CIA partnership give the premise real stakes beneath the laughs.

ratings.plot: Karsten apparently has it settled. However, in this provincial German town, a moment of weakness turns to disaster, disappointment soon fuels anger, justice hides behind hypocrisy, and evil gradually unfolds.

verdict.reason: A rare screening of this sharp moral thriller at Lincoln Center. Özge traces how a single moment of weakness unravels a man's life in a provincial German town.

ratings.plot: Direct continuation of Takashi Yamazaki's Godzilla Minus One.

verdict.reason: Takashi Yamazaki returns to finish what he started—essential for anyone who saw Minus One. A 119-minute continuation from the director of that film demands the big screen.

ratings.plot: After his mother's sudden death, Socrates, a 15-year-old living on the margins of São Paulo's coast, must survive on his own while coming to terms with his grief.

verdict.reason: A precise, unsentimental film about a teenager adrift after loss in São Paulo's margins. At 71 minutes, Moratto's direction cuts straight to the bone without wasting a frame.

ratings.plot: A woman narrates the contemplative writings of a seasoned world traveler, focusing on contemporary Japan.

verdict.reason: Marker's masterpiece of philosophical travel and montage demands the big screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph brings decades of accumulated texture into sharp focus.

ratings.plot: Medea is in Corinth with Jason and their two young sons. King Kreon wants to reward Jason for his exploits: he gives the hand of his daughter, Glauce, to Jason as well as the promise of the throne. In exchange, Medea and the boys ...

verdict.reason: Von Trier's stark vision of ancient tragedy demands the big screen and Metrograph's print. Seventy-six minutes of ruthless formal control over raw emotion.

ratings.plot: A devoted wife is visited by her mother, a successful concert pianist who had little time for her when she was young.

verdict.reason: Bergman's late masterpiece about mothers and daughters cuts deeper than any therapy session. Metrograph's restoration makes the chamber drama breathe on the big screen.

ratings.plot: On a dark, wet night a historic and regal Chinese cinema sees its final film. Together with a small handful of souls they bid "Goodbye, Dragon Inn".

verdict.reason: A rare Tsai Ming-liang film on a big screen is worth the trip. Metrograph's restoration captures the nocturnal textures and deadpan comedy of a cinema's final night.

ratings.plot: After being kidnapped and imprisoned for fifteen years, Oh Dae-Su is released, only to find that he must track down his captor in five days.

verdict.reason: Park Chan-wook's revenge masterpiece demands the big screen. Metrograph's DCP presentation locks in the angular compositions and color that make this film sing.

ratings.plot: In 2004, an ad director faces a turbulent Christmas weekend. In 2026, a filmmaker turns her story into a screenplay, blurring the lines between reality, fiction, and the people closest to him.

verdict.reason: Almodóvar playing with reality and fiction across two decades deserves a big screen. The layering of autobiography and invention is exactly what this director does best.

ratings.plot: Follows a musician from a family of musicians who returns to Los Angeles. A love letter to the music of the movies and the people who make it.

verdict.reason: Tony Gilroy's love letter to film music deserves the big screen. A rare theatrical celebration of how movies and musicians make each other matter.

ratings.plot: A businessman accidentally kills The Metal Fetishist, who gets his revenge by slowly turning the man into a grotesque hybrid of flesh and rusty metal.

verdict.reason: A rare DCP screening of a 67-minute cult landmark at Metrograph. Tsukamoto's body-horror visionary work demands the big screen.

ratings.plot: An anthology of 5 different cab drivers in 5 American and European cities and their remarkable fares on the same eventful night.

verdict.reason: Jarmusch's five-city taxi anthology is a minor classic worth seeing in 35mm. Metrograph's print captures the deadpan humor and nocturnal intimacy that define the film.

ratings.plot: A family heads to an isolated hotel for the winter, where a sinister presence influences the father into violence. At the same time, his psychic son sees horrifying forebodings from both the past and the future.

verdict.reason: Kubrick's formal control over dread and space is unmatched on a big screen. The 146-minute runtime forces you into the hotel's geometry and the family's descent.

ratings.plot: Blade forms an uneasy alliance with the vampire council in order to combat the Reapers, who are feeding on vampires.

verdict.reason: Del Toro transforms franchise vampires into something genuinely disturbing. The Reaper design alone demands the biggest screen you can find.

ratings.plot: In 17th-century France, Father Urbain Grandier's protection of the city of Loudun from the corrupt Cardinal Richelieu is undermined by a sexually repressed nun's accusation of witchcraft.

verdict.reason: Russell's fever dream of corruption and desire demands the big screen and the restored 35mm print. A genuinely unhinged vision that justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: In a corrupt, greed-fueled world, a powerful alchemist leads a messianic character and seven materialistic figures to the Holy Mountain, where they hope to achieve enlightenment.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for Jodorowsky's most accessible surreal masterpiece. The alchemical imagery and practical effects create a hallucinatory experience that demands the big screen.

ratings.plot: Verdi's famous opera is brought to life in this production. The immortal tale of the noble Moor and his beautiful young wife, and of his lieutenant, whose jealousy and lust for power lead him to commit the ultimate treason.

verdict.reason: Zeffirelli's operatic staging of Shakespeare's tragedy deserves the big screen. Lincoln Center is the right venue for this 1986 restoration of a classical production.

ratings.plot: When Denis Villeneuve hit the US scene with PRISONERS, who could have known he’d eventually be whispering to sand worms and communing with the desert on the biggest cinematic scale imaginable? Now Paul Atreides is an emperor, Chani is back, rebellion is brewing, and the bill for all that power has finally come due. Zendaya caps a truly impressive 2026 in the hugely anticipated finale that demands the biggest screen you can find.

verdict.reason: Villeneuve's desert epic finale demands a theater and 70mm print. This is the cinematic event that rewards the biggest screen available.

ratings.plot: In 1930s Algeria, the daily life of an indifferent Frenchman is shaken by the death of his mother and a fateful encounter on a beach.

verdict.reason: Skip this generic thriller that wastes a solid setup. Prasad never builds real suspense beyond the obvious ride-share paranoia.

ratings.plot: Burnt out by the LA adult film scene, washed-up porn star Mikey Saber (Simon Rex) heads back to his old stomping grounds in small-town Texas. After a not-so-successful attempt at reconnecting with his estranged wife, Lexi (Bree Elrod), he forms an instant connection with Strawberry (Suzanna Son). Soon he’s juggling jealous exes, new love, and drug-dealing locals, all with a smile on his face. Who says you can’t go home again? The audacious new film from writer-director Sean Baker (THE FLORIDA PROJECT, TANGERINE), starring Simon Rex in a magnetic, live-wire performance, RED ROCKET is a darkly funny and humane portrait of a uniquely American hustler and the hometown that barely tolerates him.

Zendaya caps a truly impressive 2026 in the hugely anticipated finale that demands the biggest screen you can find.

movies.title: September Songs: The Music of Kurt Weill

ratings.plot: September Songs: The Music of Kurt Weill is a fusion of film, theatre, and concert performance that reimagines the music of the German composer Kurt Weill whose songs bridged opera, cabaret, and popular music with piercing social and emotional insight. Featuring an extraordinary ensemble — Teresa Stratas, Lou Reed, Nick Cave, PJ Harvey, Charlie Haden, Elvis Costello & The Brodsky Quartet, Betty Carter, Mary Margaret O’Hara, William S. Burroughs, and more — September Songs transforms Weill’s work into a haunting collage of performance, theatre, and cinema. Each artist reinvents Weill’s legacy through their own lens, creating a living dialogue between past and present, exile and belonging, beauty and decay. Blended throughout the film are stylized “documentaries”, evocative imagery, and cinematic transitions that transform Weill’s haunting melodies and biting social commentary into a contemporary meditation on art, exile, and the human condition. The film celebrates Weill’s enduring influence on 20th-century music and culture. Through its visuals, its music and its original choreography, the film merges concert, cabaret, and expressionist cinema into a single dreamlike experience. The restoration — undertaken by Sphinx Productions with the generous support of Telefilm Canada — faithfully revives the film’s original textures, sound design, and the distinctive cinematography of celebrated German DOP Horst Zeidler, preserving a landmark of Canadian music cinema for new audiences worldwide.

Prepare for an electrifying, once-in-a-lifetime concert experience as Prince commands the stage in 3121 Las Vegas Live. At the height of his legendary Las Vegas residency, Prince delivers a breathtaking showcase of unparalleled musicianship, explosive energy, dazzling guitar work, and unforgettable performances. Blending funk, rock, soul, R&B, and pop, he tears through hits, fan favorites, deep cuts, and extended jams with the spontaneity and brilliance that defined Prince as one of the greatest performers of all time. Whether you've been a lifelong Prince fan or are discovering his genius for the first time, this is Prince unleashed, and an essential experience for every generation.

Like the famed empire that Francis Ford Coppola’s epic passion project is styled after, MEGALOPOLIS is a towering, monumental spectacle that most people will think about at least once a day. The City of New Rome is at a crossroads. At one end sits Cesar Catilina (Adam Driver), the idealistic artist striving for a utopian future, and at the other sits Mayor Franklin Cicero (Giancarlo Esposito), a powerful figure perpetuating greed, special interests, and partisan warfare. Their titanic struggle will shake the foundations of their city and lay the groundwork for a new tomorrow. As engrossing and ambitious as you would expect from the filmmaker behind THE GODFATHER and APOCALYPSE NOW, MEGALOPOLIS is an unforgettable vision that could only have come from Coppola. Of course, he didn’t do it alone, and everyone in the unbelievable cast (including Driver, Esposito, Nathalie Emmanuel, Aubrey Plaza, Laurence Fishburne, and more) delivers some of the most memorable performances of their careers.

ratings.plot: “Look at that subtle off-white coloring. The tasteful thickness of it. Oh, my God. It even has a watermark.” Before Christian Bale was the savior of Gotham, he was the chainsaw-wielding, business card-slinging scourge of Manhattan. Caught during the height of American Yuppieism in the late '80s, Patrick Bateman finds himself surrounded by friends who he hates and a culture he can’t stand. Can anyone blame him for allowing his nightly bloodlust to overflow into the day? It’s hard to imagine anyone aside from Bale lecturing a soon-to-be victim on the cultural undertones found within Huey Lewis and The News’ “Hip to be Square,” all while wearing a raincoat and holding an incredibly shiny axe. But, what now seems meant to be almost wasn’t! The role was originally offered to none other than Leonardo DiCaprio. However, due to his newfound fame within the teenaged female demographic, Leo’s managers felt that a stint as a sociopathic mass murderer might somehow taint his image. I guess a career in murders and executions isn’t for everyone. Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have to return some videotapes.

Presented in an English dub In modern-day Tokyo, three homeless people’s lives are changed forever when they discover a baby girl at a garbage dump on Christmas Eve. As the New Year fast approaches, these three forgotten members of society band together to solve the mystery of the abandoned child and the fate of her parents. Along the way, encounters with seemingly unrelated events and people force them to confront their own haunted pasts, as they learn to face their future, together. Co-written by Keiko Nobumoto ( Cowboy Bebop ) and featuring a whimsical score by Keiichi Suzuki, TOKYO GODFATHERS is a masterpiece by turns heartfelt, hilarious, and highly original, a tale of hope and redemption in the face of seemingly insurmountable odds. (GKIDS)

ratings.plot: Imagine any artist's worst nightmare of running into a crazed "#1 fan" who takes you hostage and forces you to "dance like a monkey" to play out their own sadistic fantasies. Maybe Stephen King was thinking about this when writing MISERY, a book and movie about a famous author (James Caan) who gets into a violent car accident and is then saved, coincidentally, by his "#1 fan." What unfolds is an absolute nightmare of seclusion, captivity, and abuse that reaches a boiling climax of white-knuckle suspense! This is easily one of the best King adaptions.

ratings.plot: Exploding with day-glo visuals and over-the-top gallows humor, THE TEXAS CHAINSAW MASSACRE 2 is not what audiences expected from recovering wunderkind Tobe Hooper in 1986. But that’s exactly what makes it so special. Using the surreal terror of the first movie as a jumping off point, TEXAS CHAINSAW MASSACRE 2 plays out like a deranged form of vaudeville with Leatherface as a sexually frustrated straight-man. Featuring electric performances from Bill “Chop Top” Moseley, Caroline Williams, and a chainsaw-wielding Dennis Hopper, it’s time to praise this movie for what it is—a drop-dead masterpiece of subversive 1980s horror. (American Genre Film Archive)

Based on the true story of one of America's greatest unsolved mysteries of one of its most notorious serial killers, ZODIAC is as much a story of obsession as it is a story of murder. In the ‘60s and ‘70s, the Zodiac was a serial killer in the San Francisco area who would routinely taunt the police with letters and ciphers in newspapers. One day, a young political cartoonist, Robert Graysmith (Jake Gyllenhaal), cracks one of the Zodiac’s ciphers and spirals into a sea of perpetual preoccupation with solving his riddles and finding out his true identity with the help of his co-worker/crime reporter friend Paul Avery (Robert Downey Jr.). Always intrigued by the case while growing up in the Bay Area, the Zodiac was David Fincher’s “ultimate boogeyman.” Fincher set out with his screenwriter and producer to conduct an 18-month investigation into the unsolved case while rewriting the screenplay. The result is the story of a reporter determined to get the story at any cost. New to being an investigative reporter, he becomes all-consumed by his obsession to know the truth. Somehow along the way, it seems as though Fincher and company got caught up in that compulsion and created a spectacularly layered, investigative, and riveting narrative in their attempt to find a culprit posthumously. This film was a technical marvel and a true cinematic masterpiece of Fincher’s career that, despite overwhelming positive reviews and an all-star cast, was left basically ignored by audiences. Don’t make the same mistake twice and miss your chance to get swept up in this gut-wrenching sea of anxiety!

Marina Pinares, the wife of the president of a South American country, insists on being his vice-presidential running mate in the next election. She's no stranger to assassination to get what she wants, so some suspect she'll kill her own husband after the election to become president. In a series of flashbacks we see her rise to power: a party girl willing to sacrifice a friend's virtue to gain favor; the lover of a soldier she later tortures; the mistress of the military man she soon marries. Based on the life of Eva Peron and directed by adult filmmaker Radley Metzger (SCORE, THE OPENING OF MISTY BEETHOVEN), LITTLE MOTHER is a rarely-seen tale of political intrigue that's ready for rediscovery.
